claim: Three currently available versions of mouse DNAm clocks were either created for individual tissues or tuned toward young ages.
source: Three currently available versions of mouse DNAm clocks were either created for individual tissues or tuned toward young ages.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to the three existing mouse clock papers and is further detailed in Table 1 showing their characteristics.

claim: A robust multi-tissue age predictor based on 435 CpG sites was constructed that covers the entire mouse lifespan and remains unbiased with respect to any particular age group.
source: Here, we constructed a robust multi-tissue age predictor based on 435 CpG sites, which covers the entire mouse lifespan and remains unbiased with respect to any particular age group.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by the experimental data presented in Figures 1-5 showing performance across different ages and tissues.

claim: The WLMT clock can successfully detect the effects of certain lifespan-modulating interventions on DNAm age.
source: It can successfully detect the effects of certain lifespan-modulating interventions on DNAm age as well as the rejuvenation effect related to the transition from fibroblasts to iPSCs.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5 testing various interventions including caloric restriction, GHR knockout, and Snell dwarf mice.

claim: The WLMT clock can detect the rejuvenation effect related to the transition from fibroblasts to iPSCs.
source: It can successfully detect the effects of certain lifespan-modulating interventions on DNAm age as well as the rejuvenation effect related to the transition from fibroblasts to iPSCs.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 5C showing significant changes in DNAm age during iPSC conversion.

claim: Age predictors based on DNA methylation levels at a small set of CpG sites (DNAm clocks) have been developed for humans and extended to several other species.
source: Age predictors based on DNA methylation levels at a small set of CpG sites, DNAm clocks, have been developed for humans and extended to several other species.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work on human, whale, wolf, and dog DNAm clocks.

claim: Various biomarkers of age have previously been suggested based on telomere length.
source: Various biomarkers of age have previously been suggested, which are based on telomere length (Harley et al., 1990), mutation accumulation (Dollé et al., 2000; Podolskiy et al., 2016; Podolskiy and Gladyshev, 2016), gene expression levels (de Magalhães et al., 2009) or T-cell-specific DNA rearrangements (Zubakov et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Harley et al., 1990.

claim: Various biomarkers of age have previously been suggested based on mutation accumulation.
source: Various biomarkers of age have previously been suggested, which are based on telomere length (Harley et al., 1990), mutation accumulation (Dollé et al., 2000; Podolskiy et al., 2016; Podolskiy and Gladyshev, 2016), gene expression levels (de Magalhães et al., 2009) or T-cell-specific DNA rearrangements (Zubakov et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Dollé et al., 2000; Podolskiy et al., 2016; Podolskiy and Gladyshev, 2016.

claim: Various biomarkers of age have previously been suggested based on gene expression levels.
source: Various biomarkers of age have previously been suggested, which are based on telomere length (Harley et al., 1990), mutation accumulation (Dollé et al., 2000; Podolskiy et al., 2016; Podolskiy and Gladyshev, 2016), gene expression levels (de Magalhães et al., 2009) or T-cell-specific DNA rearrangements (Zubakov et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to de Magalhães et al., 2009.

claim: Various biomarkers of age have previously been suggested based on T-cell-specific DNA rearrangements.
source: Various biomarkers of age have previously been suggested, which are based on telomere length (Harley et al., 1990), mutation accumulation (Dollé et al., 2000; Podolskiy et al., 2016; Podolskiy and Gladyshev, 2016), gene expression levels (de Magalhães et al., 2009) or T-cell-specific DNA rearrangements (Zubakov et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Zubakov et al., 2010.

claim: Previous approaches to construct a precise biomarker of age proved to be relatively limited in their potential to assess the aging process and examine its modulation by various interventions, mostly due to large variability of detected ages.
source: However, these approaches to construct a precise biomarker of age proved to be relatively limited in their potential to assess the aging process and examine its modulation by various interventions, mostly due to large variability of detected ages.
evidence: This is a comparative assessment based on established knowledge about the limitations of prior biomarkers.

claim: Analyses of DNA methylation provided an opportunity for much more accurate estimation of age of organisms compared to previous biomarkers.
source: In contrast, analyses of DNA methylation provided an opportunity for much more accurate estimation of age of organisms.
evidence: This is supported by the subsequent discussion of DNAm clock performance and citations to foundational DNAm clock papers.

claim: Age predictors based on DNA methylation were first proposed for human saliva samples.
source: Age predictors based on DNA methylation were first proposed for human saliva samples (Bocklandt et al., 2011) and were later developed into robust blood-specific (Hannum et al., 2013) and multi-tissue (Horvath, 2013) biomarkers of age.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Bocklandt et al., 2011.

claim: DNA methylation age predictors were later developed into robust blood-specific biomarkers of age.
source: Age predictors based on DNA methylation were first proposed for human saliva samples (Bocklandt et al., 2011) and were later developed into robust blood-specific (Hannum et al., 2013) and multi-tissue (Horvath, 2013) biomarkers of age.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Hannum et al., 2013.

claim: DNA methylation age predictors were later developed into robust multi-tissue biomarkers of age.
source: Age predictors based on DNA methylation were first proposed for human saliva samples (Bocklandt et al., 2011) and were later developed into robust blood-specific (Hannum et al., 2013) and multi-tissue (Horvath, 2013) biomarkers of age.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Horvath, 2013.

claim: DNAm clocks remain the most precise markers of age to date.
source: To date, age predictors based on systematic changes of DNA methylation with age, DNAm clocks, remain the most precise markers of age.
evidence: This is supported by the subsequent example of the human multi-tissue clock's precision and established knowledge in the field.

claim: The human multi-tissue DNAm clock has a median error of 3.6 years.
source: For example, the human multi-tissue DNAm clock has a median error of 3.6 years (Horvath, 2013), which does not exceed ~3% of maximal human lifespan.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Horvath, 2013.

claim: The median error of the human multi-tissue DNAm clock does not exceed approximately 3% of maximal human lifespan.
source: For example, the human multi-tissue DNAm clock has a median error of 3.6 years (Horvath, 2013), which does not exceed ~3% of maximal human lifespan.
evidence: This is a calculation based on the cited median error and knowledge of human lifespan.

claim: Human DNAm clocks reflect age acceleration associated with progeria.
source: The already developed human DNAm clocks reflect age acceleration associated with genetic background, such as progeria (Maierhofer et al., 2017), as well as caused by lifestyle and diet, such as smoking and obesity (Quach et al., 2017; Levine et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Maierhofer et al., 2017.

claim: Human DNAm clocks reflect age acceleration caused by smoking and obesity.
source: The already developed human DNAm clocks reflect age acceleration associated with genetic background, such as progeria (Maierhofer et al., 2017), as well as caused by lifestyle and diet, such as smoking and obesity (Quach et al., 2017; Levine et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Quach et al., 2017; Levine et al., 2018.

claim: Age predictors based on DNA methylation were recently constructed for whales.
source: Age predictors based on DNA methylation were also recently constructed for whales (Polanowski et al., 2014), wolves and dogs (Thompson et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Polanowski et al., 2014.

claim: Age predictors based on DNA methylation were recently constructed for wolves and dogs.
source: Age predictors based on DNA methylation were also recently constructed for whales (Polanowski et al., 2014), wolves and dogs (Thompson et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Thompson et al., 2017.

claim: Availability of DNAm clocks may help to speed up testing lifespan-extending interventions, such as rapamycin.
source: Availability of these clocks may help to speed up testing lifespan-extending interventions, such as rapamycin (Urfer et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Urfer et al., 2017 and represents a speculative application of the technology.

claim: Three DNAm clock versions have been developed for mice, including blood-based and liver-based clocks, and a young age-specific multi-tissue clock.
source: In this regard, three DNAm clock versions have been developed for mice, including blood-based (Petkovich et al., 2017) and liver-based (Wang et al., 2017) clocks, and a young age-specific multi-tissue clock (Stubbs et al., 2017) (Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Petkovich et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2017; Stubbs et al., 2017 and data in Table 1.

claim: Existing mouse DNAm clocks have been used to test the effects of several genetic, dietary or pharmacological interventions.
source: These clocks have been already used to test the effects of several genetic, dietary or pharmacological interventions (Petkovich et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2017; Stubbs et al., 2017; Hahn et al., 2017; Cole et al., 2017) on mouse lifespan.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Petkovich et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2017; Stubbs et al., 2017; Hahn et al., 2017; Cole et al., 2017.

claim: The existing mouse DNAm clocks have a limitation of tissue specificity.
source: However, the existing mouse DNAm clocks have a limitation of tissue specificity, and it also remains unclear how they relate to and perform with respect to each other.
evidence: This is an assessment based on the characteristics of the existing clocks described in Table 1 and the subsequent comparative analysis.

claim: The YOMT clock was tuned for tissues of younger mice.
source: A mouse DNAm multi-tissue clock (YOung Multi-Tissue or YOMT in what follows) was recently developed (Stubbs et al., 2017), which was tuned for tissues of younger mice, for example its mean absolute error, MAE, increased from 2.14 to 4.66 weeks if applied to animals of <20 weeks and 20–40 weeks of age, respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Stubbs et al., 2017 and the reported MAE values.

claim: The YOMT clock's mean absolute error increased from 2.14 to 4.66 weeks when applied to animals of <20 weeks versus 20-40 weeks of age.
source: A mouse DNAm multi-tissue clock (YOung Multi-Tissue or YOMT in what follows) was recently developed (Stubbs et al., 2017), which was tuned for tissues of younger mice, for example its mean absolute error, MAE, increased from 2.14 to 4.66 weeks if applied to animals of <20 weeks and 20–40 weeks of age, respectively.
evidence: This is data from the cited study (Stubbs et al., 2017) demonstrating age-dependent performance.

claim: Application of the YOMT clock to new samples required normalization of the data to the original dataset used to construct YOMT.
source: In addition, application of this clock to new samples required normalization of the data to the original dataset used to construct YOMT (Stubbs et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Stubbs et al., 2017.

claim: 76 liver, lung, brain and heart samples from 6-, 10-, 12-, 20- and 30-month-old C57Bl/6 male mice were sequenced by RRBS with 4-5 biological replicates per tissue per time point.
source: Therefore, to construct the methylation clock based on comprehensive compendium of samples, we additionally performed reduced representation bisulfite sequencing (RRBS) of 76 liver, lung, brain and heart samples of 6-, 10-, 12-, 20- and 30-month-old C57Bl/6 male mice, with 4–5 biological replicates per tissue per time point, except for two age/tissue points (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This describes the experimental data generated for this study.

claim: Only approximately 20% of CpG sites obtained by RRBS are sufficiently covered by WGBS if the same samples are sequenced by both methods.
source: While in theory whole genome bisulfite sequencing (WGBS) should include all CpG sites obtained by any other enrichment method, in reality the overlap between the results of WGBS and RRBS is such that only ~20% of CpG sites obtained by RRBS are sufficiently covered by WGBS if the same samples are sequenced by both methods (Harris et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Harris et al., 2010.

claim: Pooling together methylation profiles obtained by WGBS and RRBS resulted in too few sites covered in all pooled samples.
source: Consequently, pooling together methylation profiles obtained by the two methods resulted in too few sites covered in all pooled samples.
evidence: This is an inference based on the limited overlap between WGBS and RRBS methods.

claim: Only RRBS data was used to construct the multi-tissue DNAm clock.
source: For this reason, we used only RRBS data to construct the multi-tissue DNAm clock.
evidence: This is a methodological decision based on data availability and compatibility issues.

claim: The combined dataset of DNA methylomes included 416 samples representing 11 different tissues and cell types with 193,439 sites covered in all of them.
source: The resulting combined dataset of DNA methylomes included 416 samples representing 11 different tissues and cell types with 193,439 sites covered in all of them.
evidence: This describes the final dataset used for clock construction.

claim: The dataset was divided into training (80%) and test (20%) subsets with stratification based on tissue types.
source: The dataset was then divided into training (80%) and test (20%) subsets with stratification based on tissue types.
evidence: This describes the methodological approach for model validation.

claim: Elastic net regression with 10-fold cross-validation was performed on DNA methylomes pooled together.
source: We then performed elastic net regression with 10-fold cross-validation on DNA methylomes pooled together.
evidence: This describes the statistical method used to build the clock.

claim: The resulting DNAm clock included 435 CpG sites.
source: The resulting DNAm clock included 435 CpG sites (Figure 1, 2).
evidence: This is a key result of the clock construction, shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: WLMT is mostly (84%) based on male samples.
source: The majority of presently available RRBS samples come from male mice. Therefore, WLMT is mostly (84%) based on male samples.
evidence: This describes a characteristic of the training data.

claim: WLMT does not distinguish between male and female samples and can be applied to both.
source: Thus, WLMT does not distinguish between male and female samples and can be applied to both.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the statistical analyses showing no significant sex differences.

claim: The reported MAE for YOMT was 23.3 days.
source: The reported MAE for YOMT was 23.3 days.
evidence: This is a reported performance metric from the original YOMT publication.

claim: MAE for the 22-month-old liver samples measured by the liver clock was 4.2 months.
source: MAE for the 22-month-old liver samples measured by the liver clock was 4.2 months.
evidence: This is a reported performance metric from the original liver clock publication.

claim: On liver test samples, MAE was 69 days for WLMT and 58 days for YOMT.
source: On the liver test samples, MAE was 69 days for WLMT and 58 days for YOMT.
evidence: This is comparative performance data on liver samples.

claim: YOMT was heavily based on liver samples (44% of all samples used for training YOMT were liver samples).
source: There were two reasons for a comparatively good performance of YOMT on these samples: first, the dataset included several samples used for training YOMT, and second, YOMT itself was heavily based on liver samples (44% of all samples used for training YOMT were liver samples), unlike WLMT (23% liver samples).
evidence: This describes the composition of the YOMT training set.

claim: 23% of WLMT training samples were liver samples.
source: There were two reasons for a comparatively good performance of YOMT on these samples: first, the dataset included several samples used for training YOMT, and second, YOMT itself was heavily based on liver samples (44% of all samples used for training YOMT were liver samples), unlike WLMT (23% liver samples).
evidence: This describes the composition of the WLMT training set.

claim: The liver clock is based on methylation levels at dinucleotide positions.
source: Unlike other DNAm-based age predictors discussed here, the liver clock was based on the methylation levels at dinucleotide positions.
evidence: This describes a unique characteristic of the liver clock methodology.

claim: WLMT was more accurate than the liver-based clocks on non-liver samples with MAE of 2.69 months.
source: WLMT was more accurate than the liver-based clocks on non-liver samples (Figure 3F) with the MAE of 2.69 months, while the estimated MAE was 11.64 and 14.24 months for YOMT and liver clocks, respectively.
evidence: This is comparative performance data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: On non-liver samples, the estimated MAE was 11.64 months for YOMT and 14.24 months for the liver clock.
source: WLMT was more accurate than the liver-based clocks on non-liver samples (Figure 3F) with the MAE of 2.69 months, while the estimated MAE was 11.64 and 14.24 months for YOMT and liver clocks, respectively.
evidence: This is comparative performance data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Obtaining adequate results for the application of YOMT clock was challenging without the original training set.
source: It is important to note that obtaining adequate results for the application of YOMT clock was challenging without the original training set.
evidence: This is an observation about the practical application of the YOMT clock.

claim: The DNAm ages obtained from YOMT ranged from 88.2 to 149.5 days, while the actual range of chronological ages was between 7 and 1050 days.
source: The obtained DNAm ages ranged from 88.2 to 149.5 days, while the actual range of chronological ages of samples was between 7 and 1050 days, and overall correlation between chronological and DNAm ages was relatively low (R2 = 0.36).
evidence: This describes the limited range and poor correlation of YOMT predictions on the test samples.

claim: Overall correlation between chronological and DNAm ages for YOMT was relatively low (R² = 0.36).
source: The obtained DNAm ages ranged from 88.2 to 149.5 days, while the actual range of chronological ages of samples was between 7 and 1050 days, and overall correlation between chronological and DNAm ages was relatively low (R2 = 0.36).
evidence: This is a statistical measure of YOMT performance.

claim: YOMT clock showed good precision on samples with chronological ages approximately 3-5 months old, but lost robustness when applied to samples with more advanced chronological ages.
source: This led to a situation where YOMT clock showed good precision on samples with chronological ages ~ 3–5 months old, but lost robustness when applied to samples with more advanced chronological ages (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is an observation about age-dependent performance shown in Figure 3D.

claim: A shift in the coordinates of clock CpG sites defining the blood methylation clock was noticed and corrected.
source: We also noticed and corrected a shift in the coordinates of clock CpG sites defining the blood methylation clock (Petkovich et al., 2017) (Supplementary file 3), wherein the coordinates were accidently shifted to the next CpG site in a reported supplementary table (Petkovich et al., 2017), but not in the analyses.
evidence: This describes a correction made to previously published data.

claim: Correlation between WLMT and blood clock delta-age values was 0.42 on blood samples and 0.63 on non-blood samples.
source: Correlation between WLMT and blood clock was 0.42 and 0.63 with the blood and non-blood samples, respectively.
evidence: This is a correlation analysis of delta-age values.

claim: 31 heart, lung and hippocampus samples from an independent dataset were analyzed.
source: In addition, we analyzed 31 heart, lung and hippocampus samples from an independent dataset (Reizel et al., 2018) (Figure 4).
evidence: This describes additional validation data from Reizel et al., 2018.

claim: WLMT showed a slightly better performance than the other clocks on the independent dataset, with MAE = 53 days.
source: WLMT showed a slightly better performance than the other clocks, with MAE = 53 days while it was 58 days for YOMT, 54 days for the liver clock and 64 days for the blood clock.
evidence: This is comparative performance data on an independent dataset.

claim: On the independent dataset, MAE was 58 days for YOMT, 54 days for the liver clock and 64 days for the blood clock.
source: WLMT showed a slightly better performance than the other clocks, with MAE = 53 days while it was 58 days for YOMT, 54 days for the liver clock and 64 days for the blood clock.
evidence: This is comparative performance data on an independent dataset.

claim: YOMT and liver clocks produced tight clusters of methylation age points with standard deviation as low as 2 days for young and 3 days for older samples for YOMT.
source: Interestingly, YOMT and liver clocks produced tight clusters of methylation age points (with standard deviation for YOMT as low as 2 days for young and 3 days for older samples; for the liver clock it was 2 and 8 days, respectively) barely reflecting age change forcing us to conclude that MAE may not be a reliable assessment in this case.
evidence: This describes a limitation in the performance of YOMT and liver clocks on the independent dataset.

claim: For the liver clock, standard deviation was 2 days for young samples and 8 days for older samples on the independent dataset.
source: Interestingly, YOMT and liver clocks produced tight clusters of methylation age points (with standard deviation for YOMT as low as 2 days for young and 3 days for older samples; for the liver clock it was 2 and 8 days, respectively) barely reflecting age change forcing us to conclude that MAE may not be a reliable assessment in this case.
evidence: This describes a limitation in the performance of the liver clock on the independent dataset.

claim: Linear regressions for the residuals in YOMT, blood and liver clocks showed a significant shift of slope from 0 on the independent dataset.
source: Linear regressions for the residuals in YOMT, blood and liver clocks showed a significant shift of slope from 0.
evidence: This is a statistical analysis of systematic error in the clocks.

claim: For WLMT, the change in slope from 0 was smaller and not significant on the independent dataset.
source: For the WLMT this change was smaller and not significant.
evidence: This is a statistical analysis showing WLMT has less systematic error.

claim: The blood-based methylation clock reflected the effect of several known lifespan-extending interventions when applied to blood samples.
source: As previously reported (Petkovich et al., 2017), the blood-based methylation clock reflected the effect of several known lifespan-extending interventions when applied to blood samples (Figure 5A,B,D,E), whereas both YOMT and liver-based methylation clocks did not show a significant DNAm age-modulating effect due to the same interventions.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Petkovich et al., 2017 and data shown in Figure 5.

claim: YOMT and liver-based methylation clocks did not show a significant DNAm age-modulating effect due to lifespan-extending interventions.
source: As previously reported (Petkovich et al., 2017), the blood-based methylation clock reflected the effect of several known lifespan-extending interventions when applied to blood samples (Figure 5A,B,D,E), whereas both YOMT and liver-based methylation clocks did not show a significant DNAm age-modulating effect due to the same interventions.
evidence: This is comparative performance data on intervention studies shown in Figure 5.

claim: Only the liver methylation clock reflected a slowdown of aging in Ames dwarf mouse liver samples.
source: Only the liver methylation clock reflected a slowdown of aging in Ames dwarf mouse liver samples (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is performance data on Ames dwarf mice shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Fewer than 90% of CpG sites used by most DNAm estimators were covered in Ames dwarf samples.
source: However, fewer than 90% of CpG sites used by other DNAm estimators were covered in these samples, while in the other intervention tests all clocks had high sites representation: more than 90% for each sample and more than 95% on average.
evidence: This describes a technical limitation affecting clock performance on Ames dwarf samples.

claim: The majority of the WLMT clock CpG sites (58%) belong to open sea regions.
source: The majority of the WLMT clock CpG sites (58%) belong to open sea, 5% to shelves, 11% to shore regions of the genome, and 26% are located within CpG islands.
evidence: This describes the genomic distribution of WLMT clock sites.

claim: 5% of WLMT clock CpG sites belong to shelves.
source: The majority of the WLMT clock CpG sites (58%) belong to open sea, 5% to shelves, 11% to shore regions of the genome, and 26% are located within CpG islands.
evidence: This describes the genomic distribution of WLMT clock sites.

claim: 11% of WLMT clock CpG sites belong to shore regions.
source: The majority of the WLMT clock CpG sites (58%) belong to open sea, 5% to shelves, 11% to shore regions of the genome, and 26% are located within CpG islands.
evidence: This describes the genomic distribution of WLMT clock sites.

claim: 26% of WLMT clock CpG sites are located within CpG islands.
source: The majority of the WLMT clock CpG sites (58%) belong to open sea, 5% to shelves, 11% to shore regions of the genome, and 26% are located within CpG islands.
evidence: This describes the genomic distribution of WLMT clock sites.

claim: All autosomes were represented in the WLMT clock.
source: Interestingly, all autosomes were represented in the WLMT clock (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes the chromosomal distribution shown in Figure 2-figure supplement 1.

claim: None of the WLMT clock sites overlapped with the clock sites of YOMT.
source: We found that none of the WLMT clock sites overlapped with the clock sites of YOMT.
evidence: This is a comparative analysis of clock sites shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The overlaps between blood and WLMT and between liver and YOMT clocks were not statistically significant.
source: The overlaps between blood and WLMT and between liver and YOMT clocks were not statistically significant (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a statistical analysis of clock site overlap shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Kcns1 contained clock CpG sites present in both WLMT and blood DNAm clocks.
source: Across different genes in the mouse genome, Kcns1 contained clock CpG sites present in both WLMT and blood DNAm clocks; this gene was represented by multiple CpG sites: 6 in the blood clock and 11 in the WLMT.
evidence: This describes a specific gene with overlapping clock sites.

claim: Kcns1 was represented by 6 CpG sites in the blood clock and 11 in the WLMT.
source: Across different genes in the mouse genome, Kcns1 contained clock CpG sites present in both WLMT and blood DNAm clocks; this gene was represented by multiple CpG sites: 6 in the blood clock and 11 in the WLMT.
evidence: This describes the representation of Kcns1 in different clocks.

claim: CpG sites of the Kcns1 genomic region have a high correlation with age as shown by pyrosequencing.
source: It has been shown recently by pyrosequencing that the CpG sites of this genomic region have a high correlation with age (Han et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Han et al., 2018.

claim: CpG sites with higher weights on the RRBS-based methylation clock showed higher correlation with age measured with pyrosequencing.
source: Interestingly, CpG sites with higher weights on the methylation clock based on RRBS also showed higher correlation with age measured with pyrosequencing.
evidence: This is a comparative observation linking RRBS and pyrosequencing data.

claim: 100 new individual clocks were developed based on the same set of samples used for WLMT construction to study robustness.
source: To study robustness of the WLMT clock, we have also developed 100 new individual clocks based on the same set of samples used for WLMT construction.
evidence: This describes a robustness analysis methodology.

claim: The CpG site chr8:110168311 with the highest absolute weight was found in all 100 new clocks as well as in the blood clock.
source: Interestingly, a CpG site with the highest absolute weight, chr8:110168311, was found in all new clocks as well as in the blood clock.
evidence: This describes a highly robust clock site.

claim: The site chr8:110168311 is located in the promoter region of CALB2.
source: The site is located in the promoter region of CALB2.
evidence: This describes the genomic location of a key clock site.

claim: Three other sites from the CALB2 region were found in the WLMT clock and had high weights.
source: Three other sites from the same region were found in the WLMT clock and had high weights, making this region a good candidate for a targeted approach (Han et al., 2018).
evidence: This describes additional clock sites in the CALB2 region and cites a targeted approach paper.

claim: The CpG site chr2:164168131 appeared in 95 clocks out of 100.
source: The CpG site chr2:164168131, which appeared in WLMT and the 3-site pyrosequencing-based DNAm clock (Han et al., 2018) was found in 95 clocks out of 100.
evidence: This describes the robustness of a specific clock site.

claim: The vast majority of WLMT sites were detected in less than half of the new 100 clocks.
source: At the same time, the vast majority of WLMT sites were detected in less than a half of the new 100 clocks, supporting the notion of global methylation change during aging that allows to select different subsets of CpG sites for DNAm clocks.
evidence: This is an observation from the robustness analysis supporting a broader interpretation about methylation aging.

claim: Single-tissue-based clocks generally reflected tissue-specific age-dependent changes in DNA methylation and were simultaneously more precise when applied to the corresponding tissue samples than multi-tissue clocks.
source: Overall, we found that single-tissue-based clocks generally reflected tissue-specific age-dependent changes in DNA methylation and were simultaneously more precise when applied to the corresponding tissue samples than multi-tissue clocks.
evidence: This is a general conclusion from the comparative analysis.

claim: Multi-tissue clocks were biased toward tissues better represented in the training sets, but nonetheless better reflected systemic aging.
source: At the same time, while multi-tissue clocks were biased toward tissues better represented in the training sets, they nonetheless better reflected systemic aging.
evidence: This is a general conclusion from the comparative analysis.

claim: Most of the CpG sites with positive weight in WLMT had low DNAm levels in early life and increased with age.
source: Most of the CpG sites with positive weight in WLMT had low DNAm levels in early life and increased with age (Figure 2—figure supplement 4), and the opposite was true for the clock sites with negative weight (Figure 2—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This describes the directional changes in methylation at clock sites shown in Figure 2-figure supplements 4 and 5.

claim: Clock sites with negative weight had high DNAm levels in early life and decreased with age.
source: Most of the CpG sites with positive weight in WLMT had low DNAm levels in early life and increased with age (Figure 2—figure supplement 4), and the opposite was true for the clock sites with negative weight (Figure 2—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This describes the directional changes in methylation at clock sites shown in Figure 2-figure supplements 4 and 5.

claim: A similar pattern of DNAm drifting towards intermediate methylation states was shown for DNAm remodeling during aging.
source: A similar pattern of DNAm drifting towards intermediate methylation states was shown for DNAm remodeling during aging (Sziráki et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Sziráki et al., 2018.

claim: These observations support the idea of the DNAm clock being a representation of some global, systemic age-dependent changes in DNA methylation rather than being a tool to identify a small set of key genomic positions.
source: Taken together, these observations support the idea of the DNAm clock being a representation of some global, systemic age-dependent changes (Horvath and Raj, 2018) in DNA methylation rather than being a tool to identify a small set of key genomic positions, methylation status of which determines the methylation age.
evidence: This is an interpretation supported by the data and citation to Horvath and Raj, 2018.

claim: DNA methylation is a relatively new evolutionary mechanism to control gene expression.
source: DNA methylation is a relatively new evolutionary mechanism to control gene expression.
evidence: This is based on established evolutionary knowledge.

claim: Chordates lack CpG islands.
source: Chordates lack CpG islands (CGI), fishes and amphibians have only a small fraction of transcription start sites (TSS) containing CGI, and most of the TSS are associated with CGIs in warm-blooded vertebrates (Sharif et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Sharif et al., 2010.

claim: Fishes and amphibians have only a small fraction of transcription start sites containing CpG islands.
source: Chordates lack CpG islands (CGI), fishes and amphibians have only a small fraction of transcription start sites (TSS) containing CGI, and most of the TSS are associated with CGIs in warm-blooded vertebrates (Sharif et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Sharif et al., 2010.

claim: Most of the transcription start sites are associated with CpG islands in warm-blooded vertebrates.
source: Chordates lack CpG islands (CGI), fishes and amphibians have only a small fraction of transcription start sites (TSS) containing CGI, and most of the TSS are associated with CGIs in warm-blooded vertebrates (Sharif et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Sharif et al., 2010.

claim: DNA methylation patterns show strong tissue specificity.
source: DNA methylation patterns also show strong tissue specificity (Lokk et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Lokk et al., 2014.

claim: DNA methylation profiles change with age differently in individual tissues.
source: As a consequence, DNA methylation profiles change with age differently in individual tissues (Maegawa et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Maegawa et al., 2010.

claim: Construction of a multi-tissue DNA methylation clock cannot be reduced to a simple superposition of tissue-specific clocks, signifying the presence of a general pattern of aging in the DNA methylome.
source: Thus, construction of a multi-tissue DNA methylation clock cannot be reduced to a simple superposition of tissue-specific clocks, signifying the presence of a general pattern of aging in the DNA methylome.
evidence: This is an inference based on the tissue-specific nature of methylation changes.

claim: Most CpG sites belonging to tissue-specific DNAm clocks do not contribute to the constructed multi-tissue clock.
source: Furthermore, most CpG sites belonging to tissue-specific DNAm clocks do not contribute to the constructed multi-tissue clock.
evidence: This is supported by the overlap analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: DNAm clocks are not universal and must be recreated or at least adjusted for individual species.
source: Even though DNAm clocks presently seem to be the best available estimators of age, the downside of these tools is that they are not universal and must be recreated or at least adjusted for individual species.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of species-specific differences in methylation patterns.

claim: The first multi-tissue DNAm clock was developed for humans and was built based on 8000 samples representing 82 datasets.
source: When the first multi-tissue DNAm clock was developed (Horvath, 2013), thousands of samples processed with the same technology were already available, and the original human multi-tissue clock was built based on 8000 samples representing 82 datasets (Horvath, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Horvath, 2013.

claim: The number of mouse samples sequenced and available in the public domain is lower by more than an order of magnitude compared to human samples.
source: First, the number of samples sequenced and available in the public domain is lower by more than an order of magnitude.
evidence: This is a comparative assessment of data availability.

claim: Mouse methylome samples are subject to strong batch effects.
source: Second, these samples originate from a limited number of studies (Petkovich et al., 2017), and the associated methylomes are thus subject to strong batch effects, which are hard to separate from the tissue-specific effects.
evidence: This is an observation about data quality issues in mouse methylation studies.

claim: Performance of mouse clocks is expected to improve with the increase in the number of bisulfite sequenced mouse samples and the addition of new publicly available datasets.
source: Performance of mouse clocks is expected to improve with the increase in the number of bisulfite sequenced mouse samples and the addition of new publicly available datasets.
evidence: This is a speculation about future improvements.

claim: The already available clocks can be used to examine the effects of candidate lifespan-extending interventions and address diverse questions in aging research.
source: However, even the already available clocks can be used to examine the effects of candidate lifespan-extending interventions and address diverse questions in aging research.
evidence: This is a statement about the utility of existing clocks supported by the intervention analyses in the paper.

claim: Methylation clocks are based on chronological ages of samples.
source: Methylation clocks are based on chronological ages of samples.
evidence: This is a fundamental characteristic of how DNAm clocks are constructed.

claim: The ability of clocks to reflect interventions would support the idea that methylation clocks may measure biological ages.
source: The ability of the clocks to reflect these interventions would support the idea that methylation clocks may measure biological ages.
evidence: This is a logical inference about what intervention responses indicate.

claim: Clocks with better performance on control samples are better in detecting the effects of interventions.
source: Besides, clocks with better performance on control samples are better in detecting the effects of interventions.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the relationship between baseline performance and intervention detection.

claim: The blood clock has the lowest MAE among all clocks on untreated wild type blood samples.
source: It can be seen for the blood clock: it has the lowest MAE among all clocks on the untreated wild type blood samples (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is performance data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The blood clock can detect significant changes in lifespan-extending interventions even in cases where other clocks cannot with the given sample size.
source: At the same time, it can detect significant changes in lifespan-extending interventions even in the cases where the other clocks cannot do it with the given sample size (Figure 5A,B,E).
evidence: This is comparative performance data on interventions shown in Figure 5.

claim: WLMT and liver clocks should be used as linear models.
source: WLMT and liver clocks should be used as linear models, while YOMT and blood clock used a different approach, when DNAm data is first converted into a DNAm score, which then requires an additional transformation to reflect age (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This describes methodological differences between the clocks.

claim: YOMT and blood clock convert DNAm data into a DNAm score, which then requires an additional transformation to reflect age.
source: WLMT and liver clocks should be used as linear models, while YOMT and blood clock used a different approach, when DNAm data is first converted into a DNAm score, which then requires an additional transformation to reflect age (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This describes methodological differences between the clocks.

claim: Chronological age was directly used to construct the WLMT clock.
source: Chronological age was directly used to construct the WLMT clock, while log-transformed chronological age was used in models based on blood, liver and YOMT, making these clocks more tuned towards young ages.
evidence: This describes a methodological difference in clock construction.

claim: Log-transformed chronological age was used in models based on blood, liver and YOMT, making these clocks more tuned towards young ages.
source: Chronological age was directly used to construct the WLMT clock, while log-transformed chronological age was used in models based on blood, liver and YOMT, making these clocks more tuned towards young ages.
evidence: This describes a methodological difference and its consequence.

claim: RRBS is an enrichment method.
source: The most popular method to measure DNA methylation at many loci, RRBS, is an enrichment method.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the RRBS methodology.

claim: Some sites covered in one RRBS sample might not be covered at all in another.
source: One of its downsides is the fact that some sites covered in one sample might not be covered at all in another.
evidence: This is a known limitation of the RRBS method.

claim: Only samples with more than 2 million sites covered were selected for training the WLMT clock, representing mere 10% of all possible CpG sites covered in at least one sample.
source: We directly faced this issue in the present work and, even though only samples with more than 2 million sites covered were selected for training the WLMT clock, these 2 million sites represented mere 10% of all possible CpG sites covered in at least one sample.
evidence: This describes a data quality challenge in the study.

claim: The median number of WLMT clock sites covered in samples not used for clock construction was 435, equal to the total number of sites the WLMT clock is based on.
source: The median number of WLMT clock sites covered in the samples not used for the construction of the clock (and, thus, not pre-selected) was 435, equal to the total number of the sites the WLMT clock is based on.
evidence: This describes the coverage of clock sites in independent samples.

claim: WLMT had 75% of clock sites covered in a low-coverage dataset, leading among all clocks.
source: None of the clocks comparatively studied here had good clock site coverage in this low-coverage dataset, but WLMT was leading with 75% of the clock sites utilized.
evidence: This describes relative performance on low-coverage data.

claim: Less than 90% of WLMT sites were covered in all WGBS datasets.
source: Less than 90% of WLMT sites were covered in all WGBS datasets.
evidence: This describes a limitation when applying RRBS-based clocks to WGBS data.

claim: Blood clock sites were less represented in datasets not used for training the blood clock.
source: Interestingly, blood clock sites were less represented in the datasets which were not used for training the blood clock.
evidence: This is an observation about site coverage in independent datasets.

claim: The blood clock is the only one among those studied for which the median site coverage in the independent dataset was below 100% (87 out of 90 sites).
source: The blood clock is the only one among studied here for which the median site coverage in the independent dataset (Reizel et al., 2018) was below 100% (87 out of 90 sites).
evidence: This describes site coverage in an independent dataset.

claim: The blood clock was trained on a dataset created under the same conditions, while other clocks were trained on the overlap of multiple datasets.
source: This can be explained by the fact that the blood clock was trained on the dataset created under the same conditions, while the other clocks were trained on the overlap of multiple datasets, thus neglecting CpGs in the positions which have experiment-to-experiment variability.
evidence: This is an explanation for the observed difference in site coverage.

claim: Both multi-tissue clocks and the blood clock reflect changes of methylation age in relation to changes in chronological age in all tested tissues.
source: Comparing the clocks, we noticed an interesting phenomenon – both multi-tissue clocks and the blood clock reflect changes of methylation age in relation to changes in chronological age in all tested tissues, even though those changes are detected better in some tissues than in the others.
evidence: This is an observation from the comparative analysis shown in Figure 3-figure supplement 2.

claim: Performance of the blood clock decreases in the following order: liver, lung, heart and cortex.
source: Performance of the blood clock decreases in following order: liver, lung, heart and cortex.
evidence: This is an observation about tissue-specific performance.

claim: The liver clock performs well on liver samples but fails to reflect changes in any other tissue.
source: But this is not the case for the liver clock, another single tissue-based clock. While it performs well on the liver samples, it fails to reflect changes in any other tissue (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is an observation about the tissue specificity of the liver clock shown in Figure 3-figure supplement 2.

claim: Blood has a better representation of multiple cell types than liver, which mostly consists of hepatocytes.
source: A possible explanation for this difference can be based on the fact that blood has a better representation of multiple cell types than liver mostly consisting of one cell type – hepatocytes which are polypoid (and as such the majority of liver DNA is the hepatocyte DNA (Duncan et al., 2010)).
evidence: This is an explanation based on tissue composition, supported by citation to Duncan et al., 2010.

claim: The majority of liver DNA is hepatocyte DNA.
source: A possible explanation for this difference can be based on the fact that blood has a better representation of multiple cell types than liver mostly consisting of one cell type – hepatocytes which are polypoid (and as such the majority of liver DNA is the hepatocyte DNA (Duncan et al., 2010)).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Duncan et al., 2010.

claim: It is possible that blood better represents organismal aging than liver.
source: It is also possible that blood better represents organismal aging than liver.
evidence: This is a speculation about why blood clocks generalize better.

claim: The constructed multi-tissue DNAm clock can be applied to mice of both sexes.
source: The constructed multi-tissue DNAm clock can also be applied to mice of both sexes and may be a preferred method to study aging of tissues lacking tissue-specific clocks.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the sex comparison analysis.

claim: WLMT may be a preferred method to study aging of tissues lacking tissue-specific clocks.
source: The constructed multi-tissue DNAm clock can also be applied to mice of both sexes and may be a preferred method to study aging of tissues lacking tissue-specific clocks.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the comparative performance analysis.

claim: Tissues from C57BL/6N mice were used in the study.
source: We used tissues from the animals analyzed in our previous study (Petkovich et al., 2017) (C57BL/6N mice; RRID: MGI:5913915).
evidence: This describes the mouse strain used in the study.

claim: The right halves of cortex were homogenized prior to sampling to minimize the effect of brain heterogeneity.
source: To minimize the effect of brain heterogeneity (Lister et al., 2013), we homogenized the right halves of cortex prior to sampling.
evidence: This describes a methodological approach to address tissue heterogeneity, with citation to Lister et al., 2013.

claim: DNA was extracted using DNeasy Blood and Tissue Kit from Qiagen.
source: DNA was extracted using DNeasy Blood and Tissue Kit from Qiagen and eluted in 200 μl of 10 mM Tris-HCl buffer, pH 8.0.
evidence: This describes the DNA extraction method.

claim: RRBS sample preparation was performed using 100 ng of DNA.
source: RRBS sample preparation was performed using 100 ng of DNA following the protocol from Petkovich et al. (2017).
evidence: This describes the RRBS library preparation method.

claim: Each library was made of 3-6 samples.
source: Each library was made of 3–6 samples.
evidence: This describes the library pooling strategy.

claim: Samples were grouped into libraries distributing each group of samples into different libraries to avoid age- or tissue-related batch effects.
source: In order to avoid age- or tissue-related batch effect, we grouped samples into the libraries distributing each group of samples into different libraries (Supplementary file 5).
evidence: This describes the experimental design to minimize batch effects.

claim: The libraries were sequenced with Illumina HiSeq2500, PE150 with average 44M reads per sample.
source: The libraries were sequenced with Illumina HiSeq2500, PE150 with average 44M (Figure 1-figure supplement 4) reads per sample.
evidence: This describes the sequencing parameters.

claim: 20% of mouse genomic DNA library was spiked in to compensate for low complexity of the libraries.
source: 20% of mouse genomic DNA library was spiked in to compensate for low complexity of the libraries.
evidence: This describes a technical adjustment to the sequencing protocol.

claim: The data obtained in this study were deposited to GEO with the accession number GSE121141.
source: The data obtained in this study were deposited to GEO with the accession number GSE121141.
evidence: This provides the data availability information.

claim: The same processing pipeline was applied to all samples to ensure consistency.
source: Since data in these projects were processed differently, which could in principle affect estimated methylation levels, we utilized raw reads and applied the same pipeline to all samples.
evidence: This describes the data processing approach to ensure comparability.

claim: The reads were trimmed using Trim Galore v0.4.1 with the parameter --rrbs for all samples.
source: The reads were trimmed using Trim Galore v0.4.1 (RRID: SCR_011847) with the parameter --rrbs for all samples, --paired for the paired-end sequenced.
evidence: This describes the read trimming method.

claim: The filtered reads were mapped to the mouse genome (GRCm38/mm10) using Bismark v0.15.0.
source: The filtered reads were mapped to the mouse genome (GRCm38/mm10) using Bismark v0.15.0 (RRID: SCR_005604) with the default parameters to obtain methylation levels and coverage per site.
evidence: This describes the read mapping method.

claim: Sites in the mitochondrial genome and sex chromosomes were removed.
source: Sites in the mitochondrial genome and sex chromosomes were removed.
evidence: This describes a filtering step in the data processing.

claim: A soft coverage cutoff was applied, excluding CpG sites which had <5x coverage in more than 90% of samples.
source: We applied a soft coverage cutoff, excluding CpG sites which had <5x coverage in more than 90% of samples.
evidence: This describes a quality control filter.

claim: Custom scripts for data filtering and processing were written in R and python programming languages.
source: Custom scripts for data filtering and processing were written in R and python programming languages.
evidence: This describes the computational tools used.

claim: The scripts were deposited to GitHub under GNU General Public License.
source: They were deposited to GitHub under GNU General Public License: https://github.com/gr-meer/WLMT (Meer, 2018; copy archived at https://github.com/elifesciences-publications/WLMT).
evidence: This provides code availability information.

claim: The relation of CpG sites to CpG islands and genes was annotated using annotatr package from Bioconductor.
source: The relation of CpG sites to CpG islands and genes was annotated using annotatr package from Bioconductor (Cavalcante and Sartor, 2017) (RRID: SCR_006442).
evidence: This describes the annotation method with citation.

claim: ElasticNet regression was performed using the python scikit-learn package.
source: ElasticNet regression was performed using the python scikit-learn package (Pedregosa, 2012) (RRID: SCR_002577).
evidence: This describes the statistical method and software used.

claim: Stratification based on tissue types was applied to splitting samples into training and test sets and during 10-fold cross validation.
source: Stratification based on tissue types was applied to splitting samples into training (80%) and test (20%) set and during 10-fold cross validation.
evidence: This describes the validation strategy.
